st.t: Architectural innovation: Familiar components can displace incumbents
st.an: The source directly supports the cluster’s proposition: familiar components can be reconfigured through changed relationships in ways that disadvantage incumbents whose inherited architectural knowledge, evaluation filters and organisational structures impede recognition and implementation. It also matches the cluster’s qualified framing by treating architectural maladaptation as critical but not exclusive and acknowledging evidentiary and theoretical limits.
qs: Our analysis of the industry's history suggests                that a reliance on architectural knowledge derived from expe-                rience with the previous generation blinded the incumbent                firms to critical aspects of the new technology.

In all three cases, other factors also                 played a role in the firm's dramatic loss of market share, but                 a failure to respond effectively to architectural innovation was                 of critical importance.

kp.k: Minor technological changes can undermine established firms
kp.d: The authors argue that the incremental–radical distinction cannot adequately explain why apparently modest product changes sometimes produce major competitive disruption. Their framework concerns manufactured products and product-development organizations, not AI or legal services; its contribution is a historical and theoretical account of organizational responses to technological change.
qs: There is growingevidence that there are numerous technical innovationsthat involveapparentlymodest changes to the existing technology but that have quite dramaticcom- petitive consequences (Clark,1987).

kp.k: Architectural innovation changes linkages while preserving core concepts
kp.d: Architectural innovation reconfigures the relationships among existing components without overturning their underlying design concepts. Components may nevertheless change in size or other subsidiary parameters, creating new interactions. The framework separates component knowledge from knowledge of how components fit together, explaining how existing expertise can remain valuable while established integration knowledge becomes obsolete.
qs: The essence of an architecturalinnovationis the reconfigura- tion of an established system to linktogether existing com- ponents in a new way.
This does not mean that the components themselves are untouchedby architecturalinno- vation.

kp.k: Four innovation types describe different knowledge effects
kp.d: The authors classify innovation along two dimensions: changes to core component concepts and changes to component linkages. Incremental innovation reinforces both; modular innovation overturns core concepts while preserving architecture; architectural innovation changes linkages while preserving core concepts; radical innovation changes both. They explicitly treat these distinctions as matters of degree rather than mutually exclusive empirical categories.
qs: The matrixin Figure1 is designed to suggest that a given innovationmay be less radicalor more architectural,not to suggest that the world can be neatly dividedinto four quadrants.

kp.k: Dominant designs redirect learning toward component improvements
kp.d: The theoretical account links organizational knowledge to technological evolution. Early experimentation requires learning about alternative components and architectures. Once a dominant design emerges, competitive pressures favor deeper component expertise within an accepted architecture, reducing investment in alternative configurations. This specialization supports incremental improvement but shapes what organizations subsequently notice and understand.
qs: Successful organizationstherefore switch their limited attentionfrom learninga littleabout many differentpossible designs to learninga great deal about the dominantdesign.

kp.k: Architectural knowledge becomes embedded in organizational routines
kp.d: The authors identify communication channels, information filters and problem-solving strategies as mechanisms through which stable architectural knowledge becomes implicit. Channels reflect established component interactions, filters select information historically relevant to design, and problem-solving strategies prioritize previously successful solutions. These mechanisms improve efficiency precisely because they need not be consciously reconstructed for each project.
qs: Since in an industrycharacterizedby a dominantdesign, ar- chitecturalknowledge is stable, it tends to become em- bedded in the practices and proceduresof the organization.
The strategies designers use, their channels for communica- tion, and their informationfilters emerge in an organizationto help it cope with complexity.

kp.k: Familiar components can conceal unfamiliar architectural demands
kp.d: The first proposed incumbent disadvantage is delayed recognition. Organizations may interpret architectural innovation as incremental because familiar components suggest continuity, while existing information filters and communication channels screen out evidence of changed interactions. This differs from radical innovation, where new core concepts make the need for new knowledge more apparent.
qs: Since the core concepts of the design remainuntouched,the organization may mistakenlybelieve that it understandsthe new tech- nology.

kp.k: Recognition alone does not enable successful adaptation
kp.d: The second disadvantage is implementation: firms must shift from refinement within a stable architecture to exploratory learning, acquire new architectural knowledge, and identify which existing routines to retain or replace. Entrants also face learning costs, but the authors argue that they can organize around the new design without the same legacy commitments. Incumbents may instead modify existing organizational tools to avoid the costs and friction of replacement.
qs: Simplyrecognizingthat a new tech- nology is architecturalin characterdoes not give an estab- lished organizationthe architecturalknowledge that it needs.

New entrantsto the industrymust also buildthe architectural knowledge necessary to exploit an architecturalinnovation, but since they have no existing assets, they can optimize their organizationand information-processing    structuresto exploit the potentialof a new design.

kp.k: Historical equipment study examines the proposed mechanism
kp.d: The empirical illustration draws on a two-year field-based study of semiconductor photolithographic alignment equipment. Its core panel covers research and development costs and sales revenue by product for every product-development project conducted between 1962 and 1986, supplemented by managerial and technical histories. Over a hundred people were interviewed between March 1987 and May 1988; most interviews were semistructured and lasted about two hours. Sources included trade and scientific publications, consulting reports and internal firm records; histories were circulated to knowledgeable participants for correction. The industry was selected partly because it offered several examples of architectural innovation.
qs: Duringthe course of the re- search, over a hundredpeople were interviewed.
The study was initiallydesigned to serve as an explorationof the validityof the concept of architecturalinnovation

kp.k: Successive architectural changes coincided with incumbent leadership losses
kp.d: The study identifies four waves: contact to proximity alignment, proximity to scanning projection, scanners to first-generation steppers, and first- to second-generation steppers. The authors report that core optical lithography technologies remained largely intact, yet each transition defeated the industry leader. Reported shares of deflated cumulative sales over 1962–1986 include Canon's 67% in proximity equipment, Perkin-Elmer's 78% in scanners, GCA's 55% in first-generation step-and-repeat equipment, and Nikon's 70% in second-generation equipment. These are cumulative generation-specific shares, not annual market shares; the authors caution that products remained on sale and second-generation equipment was still early in its life cycle in 1986.
qs: In nearly every case, the established firm invested heavily in the next generation of equipment, only to meet with very little success.
Yet, in each case, the industryleaderwas unableto make the transition.

kp.k: Kasper treated proximity alignment as a routine extension
kp.d: Kasper, founded in 1968, supplied approximately half the contact-aligner market by 1973 and introduced a contact aligner with proximity capability that year. Nearly half its aligners sold from 1974 onward had that capability, but customers rarely used proximity mode; sales declined until the firm exited in 1981. Proximity alignment required substantially greater gap-setting accuracy and stability, including new relationships with other components. The authors argue that Kasper's successful contact-aligner experience diverted attention from these requirements, whereas Canon incorporated a more sophisticated understanding of the relevant interactions.
qs: Kasper conceived of the proximity aligner as a modified con- tact aligner.
Like the incremental improvements to the con- tact aligner before it, design of the proximity aligner was managed as a routine extension to the product line.

kp.k: Inherited filters distorted customer complaints and competitor assessment
kp.d: Kasper attributed many proximity-equipment problems to processing errors because these had been the main source of problems with contact alignment. It consequently devoted little attention to improving its gap-setting mechanism. Its assessment of Canon's machine likewise used contact-aligner criteria and missed the redesigned gap mechanism. The authors present these incidents as evidence of failed recognition, while acknowledging additional contributors to Kasper's decline: automatic-alignment difficulties, high-volume manufacturing problems and rapid top-management changes.
qs: The firm "knew" that its gap-setting mechanism was entirely adequate, and, as a result, devoted very little time to improving its performance.
The technical features that made Canon's aligner a significant advance, particularlythe redesigned gap mechanism, were not observed because they were not con- sidered important.

kp.k: Perkin-Elmer missed interactions despite accurate component forecasts
kp.d: Perkin-Elmer led with scanning projection aligners in the late 1970s but lost leadership when steppers came to dominate in the early 1980s. According to the authors, its engineers correctly anticipated improvements in individual components but did not recognize how interactions involving better resist systems and lens design would give steppers a decisive advantage. The case distinguishes component forecasting competence from understanding system-level performance.
qs: When evaluating the two technologies, Perkin-Elmerengineers accurately forecast the progress of individual components in the two systems but failed to see how new interactions in component develop- ment-including better resist systems and improvements in lens design-would give stepper technology a decisive ad- vantage.

kp.k: GCA's component organization obstructed second-generation stepper development
kp.d: GCA initially characterized Nikon's second-generation stepper as a copy. Even after recognizing the threat, its component-based organization and communication channels remained tied to first-generation architecture. Engineers advanced individual components but struggled to understand Nikon's optical-system integration, with few engineers responsible for those interactions. The authors attribute inadequate machine performance and lost leadership partly to this implementation problem, explicitly noting that other factors also contributed in all three detailed incumbent cases.
qs: GCA's engineers were orga- nized by component, and cross-department communication channels were all structured around the architecture of the first-generation system.
Moreover, because these changes dealt with component interactions, there were few engineers re- sponsible for developing this understanding.
In all three cases, other factors also played a role in the firm's dramatic loss of market share, but a failure to respond effectively to architectural innovation was of critical importance.

kp.k: Architectural learning may require explicit management and reorganization
kp.d: The authors suggest that learning across component and functional boundaries may require deliberate managerial attention, different skills and a different organizational form from that optimized for component improvement. They offer cross-functional teams and open organizational environments as possible responses to embedded architectural knowledge, not as tested remedies. They also propose that less-entrenched competitors may deliberately seek architectural changes to challenge dominant firms.
qs: But it may also be that learning about new archi- tectures requires a different kind of organization and people with different skills.
An organization that is structured to learn quickly and effectively about new component technology may be ineffective in learning about changes in product archi- tecture.

kp.k: Framework assumptions and broader applicability remain research questions
kp.d: The authors acknowledge that their assumption that organizational knowledge and information-processing structures mirror product structure is an approximation. They call for research on firm history and culture, whether embedded knowledge must become inert, and applicability to other industries and process innovation. Extensions to manufacturing, marketing, finance and firm-level coordination are explicitly conditional on those activities comprising interlinked components within relatively stable frameworks.
qs: We have assumed that organizations are boundedly rational and, hence, that their knowledge and information-processing structure come to mirrorthe internal structure of the product they are designing.
This is clearly an approximation.
Research could also examine the extent to which these insights are applicable to problems of process innova- tion and process development.

pts.k: Henderson and Clark argue that reconfiguring familiar product technologies can undermine incumbent firms even when the underlying component technologies remain largely intact.
pts.d: This is a cross-domain source about manufactured-product innovation, not AI or legal services. The authors distinguish architectural innovation, which changes relationships among components while preserving their core design concepts, from incremental, modular and radical innovation. Their central claim is that incumbents' architectural knowledge becomes embedded in communication channels, information filters and problem-solving strategies. These arrangements can obscure changed component interactions, lead firms to misclassify architectural changes as routine improvements, and impede implementation even after a threat is recognized. Existing component expertise therefore does not necessarily protect incumbents. Entrants may exploit the new architecture more effectively because they have fewer commitments to obsolete organizational arrangements. The authors also suggest, rather than establish, that learning about new architectures may require explicit management, different skills or organizational forms, and that less-entrenched competitors may deliberately seek architectural changes to challenge dominant firms.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The authors support their framework with historical field research in semiconductor photolithographic alignment equipment, supplemented by earlier industry experience and organizational-learning literature.
pts.d: The study assembled project-level research-and-development costs and sales revenues for product-development projects conducted between 1962 and 1986, alongside technical and managerial histories. Interviews conducted from March 1987 to May 1988 involved more than 100 participants, including engineers, marketing executives and other industry observers. Sources included internal records, trade and scientific publications, and consulting reports. Product-development and technical histories were circulated to knowledgeable participants for correction. The authors describe four waves of architectural innovation associated with leadership passing to entrants. Kasper treated proximity alignment as a modification of contact alignment, misinterpreted customer problems and failed to recognize the significance of Canon's redesigned gap mechanism. Perkin-Elmer anticipated component improvements but underestimated interactions favoring steppers. GCA's component-based organization impeded its understanding and implementation of the interactions underpinning Nikon's superior performance. The authors acknowledge that other factors contributed to these firms' declines. Their organizational and strategic propositions also draw on prior research and examples involving copiers, radios, aircraft and automotive materials; the paper does not present AI evidence or legal-market findings.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The claims concern historical technological transitions and conditional organizational mechanisms, not a dated forecast of AI adoption or legal-market disruption.
pts.d: Published in 1990, the paper's main empirical coverage is 1962–1986, with interviews in 1987–1988. The proposed mechanism is especially relevant after a dominant product design stabilizes and firms specialize in component improvements while managing architectural knowledge implicitly. Architectural innovation then changes interactions that existing organizational routines take for granted. Recognition and rebuilding knowledge require time and resources, but the authors offer no universal transition duration. They treat innovation categories as matters of degree, not sharply separated boxes. They explicitly identify bounded rationality, the correspondence between product and organizational structure, and the inertia of embedded architectural knowledge as assumptions deserving further investigation. Generalization to other industries and to process innovation remains a research question. Their cumulative-sales table is also qualified because products were still being sold, particularly second-generation steppers, whose life cycle was still at an early stage in 1986.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The principal affected groups are incumbent manufacturers, entrant competitors and engineering organizations responsible for integrating product components.
pts.d: Incumbents may lose market share or leadership despite technical experience and substantial investment in succeeding product generations. Entrants can gain advantage by organizing around the new architecture rather than modifying arrangements inherited from an earlier design. Component-specialist engineers and their managers face a changed learning task: understanding cross-component interactions rather than solely advancing individual components. In the photolithography cases, Kasper, Perkin-Elmer and GCA lost competitive position, while Canon, GCA and Nikon respectively benefited from transitions. Equipment users experienced differences in accuracy, performance, yield and throughput, making system integration commercially consequential. The authors tentatively extend their framework beyond product development to organizational tasks involving interlinked components, including manufacturing, marketing and finance. They make no claims about lawyers, law firms, legal clients or access to justice.
